Fundamentals, explained

What Is Revenue Growth?

Whether a company is making more money each year — and why that momentum matters.

So what is it, exactly?

Picture this: a food truck that sold $80,000 of tacos last year and $100,000 this year. Nothing else changed — same truck, same corner — but 25% more money came through the window. That's revenue growth: how much more the business sold this year than last year.

Revenue is every dollar a company brings in from selling its products or services, before a single bill gets paid. It's often called the top line, because it sits at the very top of the income statement. Revenue growth simply compares this year's top line to last year's and asks: bigger or smaller?

Why should you care?

Because growing revenue is the clearest sign that customers want what the company sells. More sales mean more people buying, more often, or at higher prices — and every one of those is good news. A company can dress up almost any number with accounting, but it's very hard to fake customers showing up.

One friendly warning: growth alone isn't the goal. A company can grow revenue by selling dollar bills for ninety cents — plenty of sales, no profit. That's why revenue growth is the first check of eight, not the whole report card.

Revenue Growth is check 1 of 8 on every StockSense report card — the Growing Revenue check. Here's what the row looks like in the app:

The grading scale
StrongRevenue growth above 10% — the business is clearly expanding
SolidRevenue growth of 3–10% — steady and respectable
WeakRevenue growth below 3% or shrinking — momentum has stalled

Let's make it real

Imagine two companies that each sold $100 million of products last year. This year, Company A rings up $115 million. Company B rings up $101 million. Same starting line — very different momentum.

Company A $115M this year vs $100M last year
+15%
Customers are clearly showing up in bigger numbers.
Company B $101M this year vs $100M last year
+1%
Barely moving — the business is treading water.

Company A has momentum; Company B has a question to answer. Maybe B is a steady giant having a slow year — or maybe customers are drifting away. Revenue growth tells you which direction the business is moving. The other seven checks tell you whether the trip is profitable.
